title: api.fit
text:
api.fit
api.fit(equations, data, family=None, latent=None, cor_matrices=None, dsep=False, dsep_only=False, calculate_waic=False, num_samples=1000, num_warmup=500, num_chains=1, thinning=1, n_cores=1, seed=0, dsep_max_obs=2000, quiet=False, dsep_equations_to_run=None, adapt_delta=0.95, fix_latent='loading')
High-level API for because-py. Fits a causal hierarchical model using NumPyro.
:param equations: List of formula strings (e.g., [“y ~ x + z + (1|group)”]). :param data: Dictionary of numpy arrays for the data. :param family: Dictionary specifying families (e.g. {“y”: “poisson”}). Default is “gaussian”. :param latent: List of unmeasured/latent variables (e.g. [“L1”]). If None, auto-detected from equations. :param dsep: Boolean, if True, computes and tests the basis set of implied conditional independencies. :param num_samples: Number of post-warmup MCMC samples. :param num_warmup: Number of warmup MCMC samples. :param num_chains: Number of parallel MCMC chains. :param thinning: Thinning interval for MCMC samples. :param seed: Random seed for JAX PRNGKey. :param dsep_max_obs: Maximum number of observations to use for d-sep tests (random subsampling) for speed. :param quiet: Boolean, if True, suppresses MCMC progress bars.
:return: A dictionary containing the fitted MCMC object and optional dsep results.

title: Changelog
text:
All notable changes to because_py are documented in this file.
The format is based on Keep a Changelog, and this project adheres to Semantic Versioning.






Modular Model Compiler:

Factored the monolithic compiler.py into dedicated, single-responsibility components under because.builder.components:

variances.py: Universal variance component partitioning (Dirichlet/Beta) and MAG induced residual correlations (LKJ Cholesky).
multiscale.py: Deterministic node evaluation (I(...), interactions) and cross-scale hierarchical bridging (coarse-to-fine broadcasting, fine-to-coarse resolution locking via segment_sum).
random_effects.py: Spectral Gaussian marginalization in phylogenetic eigenbases and structural random intercept/slope plates with Cholesky factors.
likelihoods.py: Distribution mapping for all 8 supported families (Gaussian, Poisson, Bernoulli/Binomial, NegativeBinomial2, ZIP, ZINB, Categorical, OrderedLogistic) and missing data (NaN) marginalization/imputation.

Decoupled self-contained Python source string generation into because.builder.codegen.

Decoupled Engine & Public API:

Slimmed api.py into a lightweight facade (~240 lines, down from 896), delegating to dedicated submodules:

because.engine.env: JAX threadpool limits (OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL, XLA_FLAGS), cgroup/SLURM/PBS/LSF core auto-detection, and lazy JAX/NumPyro initialization.
because.engine.runner: MCMC kernel configuration (NUTS, DiscreteHMCGibbs for discrete sites) and parallel/sequential execution.
because.engine.ensemble: MultiPhylo wave ensemble runner leveraging jax.pmap across available devices.
because.diagnostics.waic: WAIC calculation and pointwise log-likelihood accumulation across standard and ensemble models.
because.dsep.runner: D-Separation and M-Separation testing loop with automated subsampling and convergence diagnostics.
because.summary: Tabular posterior and d-separation summaries (summary(), dsep_summary()).


Standardized Pytest Suite & Hygiene:

Eliminated 24 root-level test scripts and obsolete debug scratch files.
Established a formal test suite under tests/ with pytest.ini and tests/conftest.py:

tests/unit/: Fast unit tests (< 1.5s) covering parser, DAG/MAG topology, and compiler codegen without MCMC overhead.
tests/integration/: End-to-end NUTS MCMC tests covering DAG/MAG d-separation, deterministic nodes, correlated errors, multiscale resolution locking, WAIC, and summaries.


R / Reticulate Compatibility:

Full backward compatibility for R’s reticulate caller, preserving function signatures, return structures, and internal helper symbols. Exposes __version__ = "1.0.0".










MultiPhylo Wave Ensemble Sampling: Parallel MCMC sampling across phylogenetic tree ensembles using jax.pmap waves.
Tree Index Parameter Monitoring: Injected 1-based K_tree_<struct> parameter into posterior samples for trace diagnostics.
ROPE Sample Preservation: Preserved raw posterior sample draws in dsep_results for region of practical equivalence (ROPE) analysis in R.
Level Disambiguation: Resolved variable and structure level disambiguation when hierarchical scales share equal sample sizes.





Omitted redundant sigma_tot and sigma_struct for latent indicator variables.
Excluded latent indicator variables from Pagel’s \(\lambda\) calculation.









Refined latent indicator exclusions in induced correlation sets.
Enhanced MCMC parameter alias mapping and kwargs forwarding.









Mean-centered group random effects in NumPyro builder to prevent confounding with global intercepts.
Support for parameter aliases, kwargs forwarding, and fit_numpyro_model alias.
Added max_treedepth and adapt_delta control arguments to fit().





Fixed NetworkX cycle and string iteration bugs when latents are passed as strings.
Graceful handling of evaluation errors for unused computed variables in hierarchical DAGs.









Universal Variance Component Partitioning: Dirichlet / Beta prior partitioning for variables with multiple competing error components (residual, spatial GP, induced correlation).
Non-Centered Parameterization (NCP) for multivariate latent errors in MAG models.
Lazy JAX/NumPyro initialization with automatic CPU core detection (SLURM, PBS, cgroups) and thread limits.









MAG Induced Correlations: Support for unmeasured latent confounders using 2×2 LKJ Cholesky correlation priors.
DiscreteHMCGibbs & MultiPhylo: Analytical spectral Gaussian marginalization for multiPhylo trees in dcat mode.
WAIC Diagnostics: Rao-Blackwellized WAIC calculations for models with discrete tree mixtures.
Summary APIs: Added summary() and dsep_summary() returning formatted pandas DataFrames.









Formula-driven SEM compilation to NumPyro models.
Topological DAG sorting and minimal d-separation basis set generation.
NUTS sampling via JAX.
Support for Gaussian, Poisson, Binomial, and Negative Binomial likelihoods.
Random intercepts and spatial/phylogenetic covariance matrix support via Cholesky decomposition.

title: Using because-py directly in Python
text: because-py exposes a fit() function that accepts formula strings and NumPy arrays. This is useful when you want to integrate causal modelling into a Python pipeline (e.g., alongside pandas, scikit-learn, or ArviZ).

title: Using because-py directly in Python
text: because-py exposes a fit() function that accepts formula strings and NumPy arrays. This is useful when you want to integrate causal modelling into a Python pipeline (e.g., alongside pandas, scikit-learn, or ArviZ).

title: Using because-py directly in Python
text:
Basic usage
import because
import numpy as np

# Simulate some data
import because
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n   = 1000
x   = rng.normal(size=n)
k   = 0.5 * y + rng.normal(size=n)
y   = 0.7 * x + rng.normal(size=n)

result = because.fit(
    equations   = ["y ~ x","k ~ y"],
    data        = {"x": x, "y": y,"k":k},
    num_samples = 2000,
    num_warmup  = 1000,
    num_chains  = 3       
)

# Posterior summary
import arviz as az
idata = az.from_numpyro(result["mcmc"])
print(az.summary(idata, var_names=["beta_y_x", "alpha_y"]))

# Or with the convienience function because.summary()
because.summary(result)

title: Using because-py directly in Python
text:
Specifying families
Pass a family dictionary to use non-Gaussian likelihoods:
#Simulate count data
log_lambda = 0.2 + (0.4 * x)
z_counts = rng.poisson(lam=np.exp(log_lambda))

result2 = because.fit(
    equations   = ["y ~ x", "k ~ y","z ~ x"],
    data        = {"x": x, "y": y, "k":k,"z": z_counts},
    family      = {"z": "poisson"},
    num_samples = 2000,
    num_warmup  = 1000,
    num_chains  = 3 
)

because.summary(result2)
Supported families: "gaussian", "poisson", "binomial", "negbinomial", "ordinal".

title: Using because-py directly in Python
text:
D-separation testing
dsep_result = because.fit(
    equations   = ["y ~ x", "k ~ y","z ~ x"],
    data        = {"x": x, "y": y, "k":k,"z": z_counts},
    family      = {"z": "poisson"},
    num_samples = 2000,
    num_warmup  = 1000,
    num_chains  = 3,
    dsep      = True,
    dsep_only = True   #skip path coefficient estimation, only run d-sep tests
)

because.dsep_summary(dsep_result)

text:
Accessing the generated model code
# Print the auto-generated NumPyro model
print(result["model_code"])
quit

title: Using because-py via R (reticulate)
text:
Overview
The because R package calls because-py transparently whenever you specify engine = "numpyro". You do not need to write any Python code — reticulate handles the bridge. The workflow is identical to a JAGS run: same formula syntax, same summary() and plot_dag() methods.

title: Using because-py via R (reticulate)
text:
A benchmark model
To demonstrate the speed advantages of the NumPyro engine, we will run the phylogenetic structural equation model (Model 8) from von Hardenberg and Gonzalez-Voyer (2025) using the Rhinogradentia dataset.
library(because)
library(because.phybase)

data(rhino.dat)
data(rhino.tree)

sem8_eq <- list(
    LS ~ BM,
    NL ~ BM + RS,
    DD ~ NL
)

Running with JAGS (Default)
Let’s start running the model with the default JAGS engine
start.time <- Sys.time()
fit_jags <- because(
    equations = sem8_eq,
    data = rhino.dat,
    structure = rhino.tree,
    id_col = "SP",
    engine = "jags", #default, so you could also omit this argument
    parallel = TRUE,
    n.cores = 3,
    n.chains = 3,
    n.iter = 12500, 
    n.burnin = 2500,
    n.thin = 10 
)
time_diff <- Sys.time() - start.time
time_diff
# Time difference of 2.284368 mins
Note: The above values for n.iter, n.burnin and n.thin are the default values for JAGS in the because package, and they were chosen to achieve an effective sample size of ~3,000 for all parameters (with 3 chains).


Running with NumPyro
The NumPyro engine compiles the model to JAX, leveraging Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation and the highly efficient No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS).
start.time <- Sys.time()
fit_numpyro <- because(
    equations = sem8_eq,
    data = rhino.dat,
    structure = rhino.tree,
    id_col = "SP",
    engine = "numpyro", #switch to the NumPyro engine
    parallel = TRUE,
    n.cores = 3,
    n.chains = 3,
    n.iter = 2000,
    n.warmup = 1000,
    n.thin = 1 #no thinning needed with numpyro
)
time_diff2 <- Sys.time() - start.time
time_diff2
# Time difference of 19.33303 secs
Note: The above values for n.iter, n.warmup and n.thin are the default values for NumPyro in the because package, and they were chosen to achieve an effective sample size of ~3,000 for all parameters (with 3 chains). The NumPyro engine does not require thinning due to the efficiency of the NUTS sampler, so n.thin is by default set to 1.


Identical Estimates, Superior Efficiency
Both engines arrive at mathematically equivalent parameter estimates, but NumPyro’s NUTS sampler is vastly more efficient per-iteration.
To achieve an effective sample size (n.eff) of ~3,000 using JAGS (which defaults to thin = 10), we had to run 12,500 iterations, which took approximately 137 seconds to compute on a Macbook Air M2. with 24 GB RAM.
In contrast, NumPyro achieved the same massive n.eff in just 19 seconds with only 2,000 iterations per chain!

A Note on Sampling Efficiency: If you look closely at the outputs above, you will notice that while NumPyro generates massive effective sample sizes (n.eff) for the beta regression coefficients, JAGS appears slightly more efficient at sampling the variance components (sigma) and phylogenetic signals (lambda). This highlights a difference in the respective samplers architecture: JAGS uses highly optimized, conjugate Gibbs updates for variance parameters, whereas NumPyro’s NUTS (Hamiltonian Monte Carlo) uses gradient-based trajectories that must navigate complex geometries. However, because NumPyro’s JAX compilation is so incredibly fast, it still generates more effective samples per second across the board. In this example, JAGS generates ~13 effective lambda samples per second and ~21.8 beta samples per second, while NumPyro generates ~34.5 effective lambda samples per second and ~165.7 effective beta samples per second.

title: Using because-py via R (reticulate)
text:
Including uncertainity in trees
NumPyro truly shines when handling more complex causal models, for example models that incorporate phylogenetic uncertainty across multiple trees (multiPhylo).
While JAGS struggles with indexing into large 3D arrays of precision matrices and evaluating the determinant dynamically at every MCMC step, the because_py NumPyro engine implementation in because handles multiple trees marginalising out the discrete tree index and evaluating all trees simultaneously during the NUTS trajectory using the DiscreteHMCGibbs sampler of NumPyro. This approach is orders of magnitude faster than the naive JAGS implementation, which requires a separate MCMC run for each tree.
In the following example, we simulate 10 trees for the same 100 species and run the same model across all 10 trees simultaneously using again both the JAGS and the NumPyro engines.
# Simulate 10 trees for the 100 species using the 'ape' package
library(ape)
data(rhino.tree)
set.seed(123)

# Create an empty list to hold our trees
trees_list <- list()

# Generate 10 trees by perturbing the branch lengths of the original tree
for(i in 1:10) {
  perturbed_tree <- rhino.tree
  
  # Multiply each branch length by a random value between 0.8 and 1.2 (+/- 20% noise)
  noise <- runif(length(perturbed_tree$edge.length), min = 0.8, max = 1.2)
  perturbed_tree$edge.length <- perturbed_tree$edge.length * noise
  
  trees_list[[i]] <- perturbed_tree
}

# Convert the list to a formal multiPhylo object
multi_tree <- structure(trees_list, class = "multiPhylo")

# Assign the exact same species names to the tips of our simulated trees
for (i in 1:10) {
  multi_tree[[i]]$tip.label <- rhino.tree$tip.label
}

#run the multi tree model using JAGS (this will be very slow)

system.time <- Sys.time()
fit_multi_numpyro <- because(
    equations = sem8_eq,
    data = rhino.dat,
    structure = multi_tree,
    id_col = "SP",
    engine = "jags",
    parallel = TRUE,
    n.cores = 3,
)
time_diff_multi_jg <- Sys.time() - system.time
time_diff_multi_jg
# Time difference of 9.70127 mins

#Now run the same multi-tree model using the NumPyro engine (this will be very fast) 
system.time <- Sys.time()
fit_multi_numpyro <- because(
    equations = sem8_eq,
    data = rhino.dat,
    structure = multi_tree,
    id_col = "SP",
    engine = "numpyro",
    parallel = TRUE,
    n.cores = 3,
)
time_diff_multi_py <- Sys.time() - system.time
time_diff_multi_py
# Time difference of 21.40381 secs

title: Installation & Setup
text: because-py is the Python NumPyro backend for the R because package. It can be used from R (the recommended approach) or directly in Python.

title: Installation & Setup
text: because-py is the Python NumPyro backend for the R because package. It can be used from R (the recommended approach) or directly in Python.

title: Installation & Setup
text:
From R (recommended)

Step 1 — Install the because R package
# Stable release
remotes::install_github("because-pkg/because@v1.9.0")

# Latest development version
remotes::install_github("because-pkg/because")


Step 2 — Install reticulate
install.packages("reticulate")


Step 3 — Install Python (if needed)
If you do not already have Python on your system, reticulate can install Miniconda for you (skip this if Python is already installed):
reticulate::install_miniconda()


Step 4 — One-step setup
because provides a built-in helper that installs all required Python packages (numpyro, jax, jaxlib, networkx, funsor, and because_py) into your active Python environment:
install_because_numpyro()
The function automatically detects your active Python environment — including RStudio project-level virtual environments (.venv) and any existing reticulate configuration — falling back to "r-reticulate" if none is found.


Troubleshooting: wrong Python environment
If in a fresh R session reticulate picks up a different Python environment than the one where the packages were installed, because will throw:
Error: Failed to import python module 'because.api'.
Python is currently running from: /path/to/wrong/python
Ensure because_py is installed in this exact environment.
Try running: install_because_numpyro()
In this case, point reticulate to the correct environment before calling because():
reticulate::use_virtualenv("r-reticulate", required = TRUE)

title: Installation & Setup
text:
Directly in Python
pip install git+https://github.com/because-pkg/because_py.git
Or from source:
git clone https://github.com/because-pkg/because_py.git
cd because_py
pip install -e .

title: because_py
text:
because_py is the Python inference engine behind the R because package. It translates structural equation models (SEMs) specified as R-style formulas into fully probabilistic NumPyro models and samples them with HMC/NUTS.
You can use because-py in two ways:

title: because_py
text:
Installation
See the Installation & Setup article for full instructions.
pip install git+https://github.com/because-pkg/because_py.git

title: because_py
text:
How it works
because_py parses SEM formulas into a directed acyclic graph (DAG), topologically sorts the nodes, and generates a NumPyro model closure on the fly. The model is then sampled with NUTS (No-U-Turn Sampler) via JAX — supporting CPU, GPU, and TPU backends.
For a full description of the statistical framework, see the because package documentation.

builder.compiler.NumPyroBuilder.generate_model_code_string(data_shapes=None)
Returns a self-contained, executable Python source string that represents the NumPyro model built by generate_model_function().
The output is intended for inspection, auditing, or copy-paste modification in a standalone Python script. Covariance / Cholesky matrices are referenced as arguments so the function signature matches what because-py passes internally.
:param data_shapes: Optional dict mapping variable names to their shapes (e.g. {“Brain”: (678,), “phy”: (678, 678)}). Used to annotate the function signature with dimension comments. :return: str — a Python source string.



builder.compiler.NumPyroBuilder.generate_model_function(data_for_compilation=None, force_plate_obs=False)
Returns a callable python function representing the NumPyro model. :param data_for_compilation: Optional dict of the data to statically optimize the JAX trace (e.g. for NaN masking). :param force_plate_obs: If True, forces the use of numpyro.plate for observations even if multiPhylo is detected. Used for WAIC calculation.
